units.title: How Language Models Work
units.outcome: Explain how training changes a model and how that model generates an answer.
units.activity: Trace one answer through tokenisation and generation, then propose changes for new Sunday hours, brief answers and live catalogue availability. Explain where information goes, whether parameters change, required materials and a test. Add one material needed to investigate original training.
units.criteria: Explain the generation loop and fixed weights during ordinary inference. Distinguish request context, retrieval, training and tool execution; connect each intervention to necessary materials and an appropriate test. Explain a researcher’s additional need.

units.title: Why Anyone Builds Open Models
units.outcome: Compare two explanations for a release decision using evidence and alternatives.
units.activity: For fictional Lantern, compare the hosting-demand explanation with the recruiting explanation. Use one named author’s framework and one limitation of it. Specify the evidence you would seek, a plausible counterargument and a condition under which you would revise your preferred explanation.
units.criteria: A defensible comparison states that managed hosting and recruitment are hypotheses, not observed motives. Product revenue linked to released models would support the hosting explanation; hiring outcomes and research collaboration would support recruitment. Either may coexist with competitive strategy. The best answer identifies evidence that separates explanations and acknowledges what public statements cannot reveal. Agreement with Gurley, Zuckerberg, Catalini or Lambert is not a grading criterion.
outcomes: Compare two explanations for a release decision using evidence and alternatives.
Distinguish an author’s strategic argument from a documented action or private motive.
Identify an observation that would change a preferred explanation.

units.title: Risk, Safety and the Data Commons
units.outcome: Analyse a release against an explicit baseline and threat model.
units.activity: For the fictional defect-explanation model, write a release assessment naming an actor, a harmful goal at a high level, existing alternatives, possible added capability or scale, a mitigation, and the evidence still needed. Include one potential defensive benefit and one data-permission uncertainty. Do not provide instructions for misuse.
units.criteria: A good answer might compare novice access before and after release, including hosted alternatives, and ask whether independent deployment meaningfully changes skill requirements or monitoring. A staged evaluation can test an uncertain capability; defensive access may improve auditing. Neither benefit cancels the risk automatically. Data provenance and terms require their own review. Grade the explicit baseline, mechanism, evidence and uncertainty, not a predetermined release-or-withhold conclusion.
outcomes: Analyse a release against an explicit baseline and threat model.
Distinguish observed misuse, capability tests and marginal risk.
Evaluate data-access constraints without confusing availability with permission.

units.title: The Lineage of Open Models
units.outcome: Compare two historical milestones using dated primary documents.
units.activity: Compare Pythia and OLMo using the linked abstracts. Make a two-row record with initial paper date, inspected version date, reported artefacts, one enabled investigation and one remaining constraint. Then write a sentence about what changed without asserting that either project is universally more open.
units.criteria: Pythia’s first paper date is 3 April 2023; the inspected revision is 31 May. OLMo’s first paper date is 1 February 2024; the inspected revision is 7 June. Pythia highlights a controlled suite and intermediate checkpoints; OLMo describes data and training/evaluation code with weights. Both support research beyond a hosted interface. Resource needs and version-specific permissions still need checking. Credit any well-supported comparison; do not grade by a ranking of the projects.

Explain what an artefact release enabled and what it left unknown.
Distinguish a publication date, a release date and later retrospective interpretation.

units.title: US–China Competition
units.outcome: Critique an adoption claim by identifying its denominator, coverage and date.
units.activity: Rewrite the Bridge headline into a defensible two-sentence claim. Identify the measure, population and dates. Give one quality-based explanation and one alternative, then propose an observation that would help distinguish them. Explain why neither statement determines a country’s overall technical lead.
units.criteria: A defensible claim says Eastbank-developed models represented 60% of Bridge’s measured June token volume, compared with 40% in May, under stated counting rules. The source does not cover global use. Quality gains could attract users; discounts and defaults could also change the mix. Compare task-level outcomes and adoption where prices/defaults were unchanged. Credit clear scope, a counterargument and a useful next check; no preferred national conclusion is required.
outcomes: Critique an adoption claim by identifying its denominator, coverage and date.
Compare a structural explanation with a plausible alternative.
Separate nationality, capability, commercial adoption and policy status.

units.title: Measuring the Gap
units.outcome: Calculate a score and a threshold delay from a small documented example.
units.activity: Recalculate the equal and 80%-manual averages for Alder and Birch. Calculate both threshold delays. Explain why “Birch wins” and “Alder fits our manual-heavy workload better” can both follow from these data. Propose one further evaluation and one limitation that would enter your memo.
units.criteria: Equal means are Alder 60 and Birch 70. Manual-heavy means are 0.8×80+0.2×40=72 and 0.8×60+0.2×80=64. Delays are 4−0=4 and 7−1=6 months. The ranking depends on the task weights; the delays answer another question entirely. Test held-out manuals representative of your organisation, inspect consequential errors and repeat unstable runs. The invented sample cannot justify a claim about real models or market trends.
outcomes: Calculate a score and a threshold delay from a small documented example.
Explain how evaluation and aggregation choices change a comparison.
Specify evidence needed before applying a benchmark result to a decision.

units.title: Distillation and Synthetic Data
units.outcome: Trace teacher–student information flow and locate the training stage.
units.activity: Draw two Willow → Juniper workflows: teacher-written answers and teacher feedback on student-written answers. Label the training stage. Design one controlled test of the benefit of teacher explanations. Then write one sentence accurately attributing the Anthropic report without converting its allegations into a proved effect size.
units.criteria: Your diagrams should identify prompts, generated material or feedback, and the student weight update. For the test, use a shared base, matched training conditions and held-out tasks; compare explanations with an answer-only control, reporting token-budget differences. “Anthropic alleged abusive collection by named labs” is supportable as attribution. “That collection caused their capability gain” requires additional evidence. Reward a clear alternative explanation and an explicit uncertainty, not agreement with either company or commentator.
outcomes: Trace teacher–student information flow and locate the training stage.
Separate a company allegation from demonstrated causal uplift.
Design a controlled comparison of teacher-assisted training.

units.title: Security, Cyber and the Regulatory Fight
units.outcome: Classify an incident report, proposal, enacted rule and forecast separately.
units.activity: Write a two-column comparison of the fictional release gate and observatory for the public-service objective. Include the actor, mechanism, baseline, enforcement, likely displacement, one cost and two success measures. Recommend one approach or a combination, then name the strongest objection and a trigger for revising it.
units.criteria: Both options must target the same harm and time horizon. A gate needs a meaningful capability threshold and review process; an observatory needs access to useful evidence and authority or funding to act. A combined recommendation is defensible only if you explain the role of each. A single approach is defensible if it addresses its strongest limitation. Treat a forecast as a forecast and reward explicit revision conditions, not the preferred politics of any author.
outcomes: Classify an incident report, proposal, enacted rule and forecast separately.
Compare two policy approaches against the same objective.
Specify success measures, displacement risks and a revision trigger.

units.title: Synthesis: Where This Goes
units.outcome: Integrate release, evaluation, cost and risk evidence into a conditional recommendation.
units.activity: Write the memo for the study-guide case, score it against the rubric and revise its weakest-supported sentence. Add a paragraph explaining how the revision did or did not change your recommendation. Include one competing argument from the named authors without using their authority as a substitute for task evidence.
units.criteria: A complete memo chooses a feasible next step, respects the sensitive-data constraint, separates known release facts from unknown quality and cost, and proposes a test with a stopping rule. It fairly states a competing option and a condition that would change the choice. The recommendation may favour a bounded local pilot, a public-content hosted pilot, or deferral if justified. Evaluate reasoning and evidence, not agreement with an example response.
outcomes: Integrate release, evaluation, cost and risk evidence into a conditional recommendation.
Represent a serious counterargument without treating a forecast as a conclusion.
Review and revise a decision memo using explicit criteria.
